name: Marula oil

lead: Marula oil is pressed from the kernels of the marula tree (Sclerocarya birrea) of southern Africa. It is mostly oleic acid, with smaller amounts of palmitic, linoleic and stearic acids, plus tocopherols and sterols.
People use it as a moisturizing oil that leaves skin soft and hair smoother. Traditional users in southern Africa applied it as a body lotion and baby massage oil.

paras: It is applied directly or in creams as a facial oil, body oil, or hair-ends and scalp treatment, often as a final step after other skincare.
It is a plant oil with a low risk profile; people with nut allergies or sensitive, acne-prone skin may want to patch test, as with other oils.

chain: Oleic-acid-rich oil applied to skin or hair
Emollient film and fatty acids soften surface
angle.text: As an emollient oil, marula oil softens skin and smooths hair when applied. People use it as a moisturizer and hair oil.

lead: Marula oil comes from the kernels of the marula tree (Sclerocarya birrea). It is mainly oleic acid (70 to 78%), with palmitic (9 to 12%), linoleic (4 to 7%) and stearic (5 to 8%) acids, plus tocopherols, sterols, flavonoids and catechins. It is clear, light yellow and has a nutty aroma. [1]

Tsonga people of South Africa and Mozambique traditionally used it as a moisturizing body lotion for women and a massage oil for babies, and Namibian women used it for cleansing. It is also a cooking oil and meat preservative in parts of southern Africa. [1]

In modern cosmetics it is used as a face and body oil and in hair products. Published work includes a clinical perspective on its safety and efficacy and lab studies of extracts for anti-aging. [2][3]

paras: Oleic acid dominates, followed by palmitic, linoleic, stearic, arachidonic and alpha-linolenic acids, along with tocopherols, sterols and polyphenols. [1]
Tsonga and Namibian traditional uses include body lotion, baby massage and cleansing; modern cosmetic use includes body lotions and oils. [1]

A 2015 paper in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology reviews the safety and efficacy of marula oil from a clinical perspective. [2] A 2018 study profiled anti-aging potential of Sclerocarya birrea extracts in the lab. [3] A 2026 study evaluated a skin-barrier lipid made from marula-oil fatty acids. [4]
